name: ECG 1 · Foundations
blurb: Name every wave, line and lead on a normal ECG.

topics.name: What an ECG is
topics.desc: Electricity, deflections and the grid every tracing is drawn on.

cards.q:
The ECG records the heart’s electrical activity, not its squeezing.
True or false?
cards.a: True. The ECG is a recording of electrical events; contraction follows them but is not what the machine measures.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.19; Khan ch1 p.1

cards.q: In a resting heart muscle cell, the inside is
cards.a:
Negative compared with the outside

Resting cells are polarised, inside negative, maintained by membrane pumps.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.19; Khan ch1 p.4

cards.q: Depolarisation of a heart muscle cell is followed by
cards.a:
Contraction of the cell

Depolarisation releases calcium inside the cell, letting actin and myosin contract it.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.20, p.26; Khan ch1 p.2

cards.q:
Every ECG wave comes from either depolarisation or repolarisation.
True or false?
cards.a: True. These are the only two electrical processes; all the waves are manifestations of them.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.20; Khan ch1 p.4

cards.q: A wave of depolarisation moves away from the positive electrode. The deflection is
cards.a:
Downward

Depolarisation moving away from a positive electrode records a negative deflection.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.43; Khan ch1 p.3–4

cards.q: A wave of depolarisation passes at right angles to an electrode. It records
cards.a:
An up-then-down biphasic wave

The wave first approaches (positive), then recedes (negative): biphasic.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.44–46

cards.q: On ECG paper, the height of a wave measures its
cards.a:
Voltage

The vertical axis measures voltage; the horizontal axis measures time.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.27

cards.q: One small square across the paper equals
cards.a:
0.04 s

Each 1 mm small square is 0.04 s on the time axis.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.27; Khan ch2 Table 2-2

cards.q: How many large squares make one second?
cards.a:
5 squares

Each large square is 0.2 s, so 5 × 0.2 s = 1 s.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.27–28, ch3 p.125

cards.q: At standard gain, how many millimetres tall is the 1 mV calibration box?
cards.a:
10 mm

Standardisation is 1 mV displayed as a 10 mm deflection.
cards.note: Khan ch2 p.77 (ECG technique), Table 2-1

topics.name: The waves
topics.desc: P, QRS, T and U, the flat lines between them, and their names.

cards.q: Explain: P wave: the atria depolarising
cards.a: The first small, rounded wave of each beat is the P wave. It records depolarisation spreading through both atria.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.29; Khan ch1 p.8–9

cards.q: Explain: QRS: the ventricles depolarising
cards.a: The tall, spiky QRS complex records depolarisation of the ventricles. It is much bigger than the P wave because the ventricles have far more muscle than the atria.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.33; Khan ch1 p.9

cards.q: Explain: T wave: the ventricles repolarising
cards.a: The broad, rounded T wave records ventricular repolarisation. Repolarisation is slower than depolarisation, so the T wave is wider and smoother than the QRS.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.37–38; Khan ch1 p.11

cards.q: Why is there no visible wave for atrial repolarisation?
cards.a:
It is buried in the QRS complex

Atrial repolarisation coincides with ventricular depolarisation and is hidden by the much larger QRS.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.37–38

cards.q: A QRS starts upward, then dips below the baseline. The downward part is
cards.a:
An S wave

A downward deflection is a Q only if it comes first; after an R it is an S.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.35; Khan ch1 Fig. 1-9

cards.q: A QRS has a tiny downward dip, then a tall upward wave, nothing else. It is a
cards.a:
qR

Small first downward wave = q; large upward wave = R.
cards.note: Khan ch1 p.10, Fig. 1-9; Thaler ch1 p.35

cards.q: Explain: The U wave sometimes follows T
cards.a: In some people a small, often indistinct U wave follows the T wave. Its source is uncertain.
cards.note: Khan ch1 p.11

cards.q: Explain: Segments are flat lines
cards.a: A segment is the straight line between two waves. The PR segment runs from the end of P to the QRS. The ST segment runs from the end of QRS to the T. The TP segment is the baseline between beats.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.40–41; Khan ch1 p.10

cards.q: Explain: The J point ends the QRS
cards.a: The point where the ST segment takes off from the end of the QRS is the J point (junction point).
cards.note: Khan ch1 p.10

cards.q: Explain: Intervals include at least one wave
cards.a: An interval spans at least one wave. - PR interval: start of P to start of QRS - QRS duration: the QRS alone - QT interval: start of QRS to end of T
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.40–42

topics.name: The conduction system
topics.desc: SA node to Purkinje fibres, and which wave each step makes.

cards.q: Where is the SA node?
cards.a:
High in the right atrium

The dominant pacemaker cells sit high up in the right atrium.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.23–24; Khan ch1 p.6

cards.q:
The SA node firing makes a small wave just before the P wave.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Pacemaker activity generates too little voltage to be seen on the surface ECG.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.27, p.41

cards.q: The first part of the P wave mainly reflects
cards.a:
Right atrial depolarisation

The SA node is in the right atrium, so the right atrium depolarises first.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.29; Khan ch1 p.8–9

cards.q: Why does the AV node delay the impulse?
cards.a:
To let the atria finish emptying into the ventricles

The pause lets atrial contraction fill the ventricles before ventricular contraction.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.30–31; Khan ch1 p.6

cards.q: Put the conduction path in order.
cards.a:
SA node → Atria → AV node → Bundle of His → Bundle branches → Purkinje fibres

The impulse runs SA node → atria → AV node → His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.31–32; Khan ch1 p.6

cards.q:
Ordinary ventricular muscle conducts the impulse faster than the Purkinje fibres.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Myocardial cells conduct far less efficiently; the specialised conducting cells are the fast highway.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.25–26, p.31

cards.q: The septum depolarises in which direction?
cards.a:
Left to right

The septal fascicle of the left bundle activates the septum from left to right.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.32, p.36; Khan ch1 p.21

cards.q: Most of the normal QRS reflects
cards.a:
Left ventricular activation

The left ventricle is about three times heavier, so its forces dominate.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.36; Khan ch1 p.21–22

cards.q: In a lead with a tall R wave, the normal T wave is
cards.a:
Upright

Repolarisation runs opposite to depolarisation, so it also records positive in leads with tall R waves.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.46, p.72; Khan ch1 p.11

cards.q: Match each pacemaker to its usual rate.
cards.a:
SA node: 60–100/min
AV junction: 40–60/min
Ventricle: 30–45/min

The further down the conduction system, the slower the intrinsic rate.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.24, ch3 p.131

topics.name: The 12 views
topics.desc: Ten electrodes, twelve leads, two planes, and the mean vector.

cards.q: How many electrodes does a standard 12-lead ECG use?
cards.a:
10

Four limb electrodes plus six chest electrodes make 10, which produce 12 leads.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.49–50; Khan ch1 p.12, p.15

cards.q: Match each lead to its angle.
cards.a:
Lead I: 0°
Lead II: +60°
Lead III: +120°

Each angle runs from the negative to the positive electrode on the frontal circle.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.53; Khan ch1 p.12–15

cards.q: Lead aVF is positive at the legs. Its angle is
cards.a:
+90°

aVF looks straight up from the feet: +90°.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.53–54; Khan ch1 p.14–15

cards.q: Order the limb leads by angle, from −150° to +120°.
cards.a:
aVR → aVL → I → II → aVF → III

aVR −150°, aVL −30°, I 0°, II +60°, aVF +90°, III +120°.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.51–56; Khan ch1 p.16

cards.q: Name the three inferior leads.
cards.a:
II, III, aVF

II, III and aVF view the inferior surface of the heart.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.55; Khan ch1 p.15

cards.q: Match each electrode to its position.
cards.a:
V1: 4th space, right sternal edge
V2: 4th space, left sternal edge
V4: 5th space, midclavicular line
V6: Midaxillary line, level with V4

These four landmarks fix the chest leads; V3 and V5 sit between them.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.57; Khan ch2 Fig. 2-38

cards.q: Name the anterior leads.
cards.a:
V2, V3, V4

Thaler groups V2, V3 and V4 as the anterior leads.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.56–58; Khan ch1 p.16

cards.q: The length of the mean vector represents the
cards.a:
Voltage of the wave

A vector has direction (where current flows) and length (its amplitude).
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.59–61; Khan ch1 p.6, p.20

cards.q: The QRS vector points to +60°. Which limb lead shows the tallest R?
cards.a:
II

Lead II sits at +60°, directly facing the vector.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.48, p.68; Khan ch1 p.20

cards.q: Name the lead where P, QRS and T are all normally negative.
cards.a:
aVR

aVR points away from the normal current, so every wave is inverted.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.62, p.68; Khan ch1 p.14, p.24

topics.name: The normal ECG
topics.desc: What each wave looks like in each lead, and normal values.

cards.q: In which lead is the normal P wave inverted?
cards.a:
aVR

aVR faces away from the atrial current, so its P wave is negative.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.62–64; Khan Table 2-1, ch3 p.81

cards.q: Explain: Normal PR: 0.12–0.20 s
cards.a: The normal PR interval is 0.12–0.20 s: 3 to 5 small squares. Khan allows up to 0.22 s in adults.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.65; Khan Table 2-1

cards.q: A q wave in V6 is 0.02 s wide and 1 mm deep. Is it normal?
cards.a:
Yes: under 0.04 s and under 3 mm, a normal septal q

A septal q is normal when under 0.04 s wide and under 3 mm deep. V1 normally has no q at all.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.67; Khan ch1 p.21, p.24

cards.q: Which QRS duration is normal?
cards.a:
0.08 s

Normal QRS is 0.06–0.10 s; 0.12 s or more is wide.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.70, ch3 p.138; Khan Table 2-1

cards.q: In a normal ECG, V1 usually shows
cards.a:
A small r and deep S

Ventricular current flows leftward, away from V1, giving a dominant S.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.69; Khan ch1 p.21–23

cards.q: The normal precordial transition zone is at
cards.a:
V3–V4

R and S are about equal in V3 or V4 in the normal heart.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.69; Khan Fig. 2-2

cards.q:
An inverted T wave in V1 can be normal.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Khan lists the T wave in V1 as variable in normal people.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.72; Khan Table 2-1

cards.q: Explain: QT under half the RR
cards.a: The QT interval shortens as the heart speeds up. A rough rule: at rates of 60–100, the QT is under half the preceding RR interval. Correcting for rate gives the QTc (QT ÷ √RR).
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.72–73, ch7 p.301; Khan ch10 p.227

cards.q: Which QRS axis is normal by Thaler’s simple definition?
cards.a:
+45°

Thaler’s normal range is 0° to +90°; +45° lies inside it.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.68, ch2 p.89–90; Khan Table 2-1

cards.q: Explain: Rate from the big squares
cards.a: Count large squares between two R waves. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 large squares mean 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50 beats a minute. A normal rate is 60–100.
cards.note: Khan Table 2-2; Thaler ch3 p.125

topics.name: A good tracing
topics.desc: Layout, calibration, wrong electrodes, artefacts and the computer read.

cards.q: Why is lead II the usual rhythm strip?
cards.a:
P waves are seen best in it

Khan: P waves are best seen in II and V1, so these are used for rhythm strips.
cards.note: Khan ch3 p.82

cards.q:
If the calibration box is only 5 mm tall, the waves look half their true voltage.
True or false?
cards.a: True. At half standard, 1 mV is drawn as 5 mm, so every amplitude is halved.
cards.note: Khan ch2 p.77, Fig. 2-25

cards.q: Why should the patient lie flat?
cards.a:
Posture changes the heart’s position and the waves

Changes in posture move the heart and alter voltage, ST segments and Q waves.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.59

cards.q: Lead I shows inverted P, QRS and T; chest leads look normal. Most likely cause?
cards.a:
Swapped arm electrodes

Reversing the arm electrodes turns lead I into its mirror image; the chest leads are unaffected.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.58; Khan ch2 p.80, Table 2-1

cards.q:
Moving a chest electrode slightly to avoid hair is harmless.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Even slight misplacement can change R waves and mimic a previous infarct.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.59; Khan ch1 p.18–20, ch2 p.80

cards.q: A shivering patient’s tracing has a jittery baseline. This is
cards.a:
Muscle tremor artefact

Skeletal muscle activity from shivering is recorded as tremor artefact.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.296

cards.q: The commonest cause of a drifting baseline is
cards.a:
A loose electrode

Khan: artefacts like baseline drift are often caused by loose or poorly applied sensors.
cards.note: Khan ch2 p.77

cards.q: Which electrode is the earth that reduces interference?
cards.a:
Right leg

Khan: the right leg electrode is an earth and minimises interference.
cards.note: Khan ch1 p.15

cards.q:
A computer report of "normal ECG" can be accepted without looking at the tracing.
True or false?
cards.a: False. The computer often misses subtle abnormalities and has no clinical context.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.76
